newsitem.title: USA: Mass. utility deregulation seeks 10 pct rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Mass. utility deregulation seeks 10 pct rate cut.

text.p: Massachusetts legislators, unveiling a plan Thursday to deregulate the state's electricity industry, called for a mandatory 10 percent cut in all retail power prices across the state by January 1, 1998.

The plan, presented at the state house by the Joint Committee on Electric Utility Restructuring, also called for allowing the state's seven utilities to fully recover their "stranded costs", referring to those investments they made back in the days of a tightly regulated power market.
The proposal encourages these same utilities to sell off all their current power generating assets.
The report, citing figures from a recent Moody's Investors Service analysis of stranded costs for utilities, estimated that those costs top $5.2 billion for Massachusetts utilities.
Legislators also want the utilities to renegotiate their contracts with independent power producers that are above market rates.

"Just about all the contracts with independent power companies are significantly above the rates," New England Electric Systems spokeswoman Karen Berardino said. Her company's recent deregulation agreement reached with the Massachusetts attorney general will be subject to the legislation.
Before the measure becomes law it must pass both houses in the Legislature and be signed into law by Gov. William Weld, who introduced his own deregulation bill earlier in the session.

The bi-partisan committee with members from both the Senate and the House of Representatives said their measure went further than Weld's by guaranteeing consumers a 10 mandated rate cut and encouraging voluntary divestiture of non-nuclear generating assets by providing incentives.
